title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
why: A historical anchor for learning residual transformations and understanding deep-network optimization.
readFor: Find the residual-block definition and compare the training behaviour of plain and residual networks.
limits: Library note checked against the primary abstract and bibliographic record; this is not an independent reproduction. Image-recognition results do not validate a financial application.
exercise: Implement a tiny plain and residual network on the same small dataset; record training curves and seeds.

title: Attention Is All You Need
why: The primary architecture paper behind the Transformer learning path.
readFor: Trace attention inputs and outputs, masks, position information, and the experimental comparison.
limits: Primary abstract and metadata verified. The original translation setting differs from later decoder-only assistants; do not attribute every modern design choice to this paper.
exercise: Reproduce a masked attention calculation with three tokens and verify the future-token isolation invariant.

title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
why: Compare bidirectional representation pretraining with causal language modelling.
readFor: Identify the pretraining objectives and how downstream adaptation is evaluated.
limits: Primary abstract and bibliographic record verified; benchmark claims are author-reported. Bidirectionality does not imply permission to use future information in a trading prediction.
exercise: Explain which token positions an encoder may access and why a causal forecasting task needs a different information boundary.

title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
why: A clear source for separating demonstrations in a prompt from task-specific weight updates.
readFor: Compare zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot evaluation, including methodological limitations.
limits: Primary abstract verified. Performance claims refer to the paper’s models and tasks; the library has not reproduced them or audited its full training corpus.
exercise: Design a fixed-budget comparison of zero-shot and few-shot prompts on a sealed extraction set.

title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
why: Introduces an empirical way to relate language-model loss to model, data, and compute budgets.
readFor: Inspect the variables, fitted ranges, and assumptions behind resource-allocation conclusions.
limits: Primary abstract verified. Empirical fits are conditional on the measured setup, not universal laws or an AGI forecast.
exercise: Plot a hypothetical power law on linear and log axes; explain why extrapolation beyond measured ranges is risky.

title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
why: A useful contrast with earlier scaling recommendations: resource allocation changes conclusions.
readFor: Compare how model size and training-token count are varied under a compute constraint.
limits: Primary abstract verified. Do not turn a reported recipe into a universal optimal token ratio for all architectures, datasets, or inference budgets.
exercise: For a fixed illustrative ND product, compare several parameter/token allocations and state what empirical data would choose among them.

title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
why: A historical reference for demonstrations, preference rankings, and assistant-oriented post-training.
readFor: Trace which dataset supplies each learning signal and how human preference is measured.
limits: Primary abstract verified. Human preference is not identical to factual truth; the authors also report remaining mistakes. No independent reproduction is claimed here.
exercise: Create separate rubrics for helpfulness, factual support, and valid tool use on the same five answers.

title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
why: An alternative perspective on learning from preferred and rejected responses.
readFor: Read the objective, reference-policy role, assumptions, and comparison protocol.
limits: Primary record verified. This library is a reading guide, not a derivation audit or proof that DPO dominates every RL-based approach.
exercise: Write a preference-pair dataset with an ambiguous example and explain how annotation uncertainty affects training.

title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
why: Provides the low-rank update idea used in parameter-efficient adaptation.
readFor: Identify frozen and trained tensors, rank choices, and the memory/performance comparison.
limits: Primary abstract and record verified. Parameter savings do not imply elimination of base-weight or activation memory. Task-specific quality still requires testing.
exercise: Calculate adapter counts for three matrix shapes and ranks; compare with base counts.

title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
why: Connects quantized base weights with adapter learning and explicit memory constraints.
readFor: Separate the paper’s quantization, memory-management, and adaptation components.
limits: Primary abstract and bibliographic record verified. Reported hardware results depend on the exact configuration; this guide does not promise those results on your device.
exercise: Build a budget table including weights, adapters, optimizer states, activations, and temporary buffers.

title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
authors: Geoffrey Hinton, Oriol Vinyals, and Jeff Dean
why: A foundational reading for transferring behaviour from a teacher to a smaller student.
readFor: Compare hard target labels with information in teacher distributions.
limits: Primary abstract and record verified. A student may inherit teacher errors; compression quality is task-dependent and requires a held-out evaluation.
exercise: Compare two teacher probability vectors with the same top class and explain what information a hard label discards.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
why: A primary reference for combining parameterized generation with retrieved information.
readFor: Separate retrieval performance from generated-answer performance and inspect the experimental tasks.
limits: Primary abstract verified. A modern production RAG pipeline can differ substantially from this paper; retrieval does not automatically ensure truthful or current answers.
exercise: Create five answerable and five unanswerable questions and score retrieval and supported answers separately.

title: Levels of AGI for Operationalizing Progress on the Path to AGI
why: A framework for making broad intelligence claims more explicit and comparable.
readFor: Examine how performance and generality are defined and where judgement remains necessary.
limits: Primary record verified; title reflects the current arXiv record. This is a proposed conceptual framework, not proof that a particular system has achieved AGI.
exercise: Classify a hypothetical highly capable but narrowly scoped tool and state which evidence your classification needs.

title: On the Measure of Intelligence
why: Challenges the assumption that accumulated benchmark skill alone captures intelligence.
readFor: Examine the roles of prior knowledge, experience, and skill acquisition in the proposed measurement view.
limits: Primary abstract and metadata verified. The conceptual position is not a universally agreed definition, and this reading guide does not independently validate every proposed benchmark.
exercise: Design two evaluations with identical final accuracy but different allowed training experience; explain why they may measure different abilities.

title: Foundations of Portfolio Theory — Nobel lecture
why: An author’s retrospective on how diversification and portfolio choice became a quantitative framework. It provides historical context for the mathematics rather than a trading recipe.
prerequisites: Expected value, variance, covariance, constrained optimization.
readFor: Identify the distinction between choosing securities individually and choosing their combined distribution. Connect the discussion to wᵀΣw and the efficient frontier.
limits: Lecture and PDF were identified through the official Nobel source; direct fetching was restricted during this audit. This is a 1990 lecture, not the original 1952 article. Historical theory does not resolve noisy expected-return estimates.
exercise: Construct two equal-weight assets with identical volatility. Vary correlation and plot portfolio volatility; explain what changes and what remains assumed.

title: The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities
why: Foundational primary research on consistent option valuation through hedging and no-arbitrage reasoning.
prerequisites: Calculus, discounting, probability, a one-step binomial replication.
readFor: Read the pricing argument before the final formula. List every market and price-process assumption needed for replication, then relate delta to the hedge.
limits: Publisher abstract verified; full text may require institutional or paid access. Do not purchase automatically. Idealized continuous hedging is not a guarantee under jumps, costs or discrete trading.
exercise: Replicate a call in a two-state model, then add a transaction cost and explain which exact-arbitrage argument becomes imperfect.

title: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting
authors: David H. Bailey, Jonathan M. Borwein, Marcos López de Prado and Qiji Jim Zhu
why: Studies how selecting a historical winner can produce poor subsequent ranking; useful for understanding research selection rather than only final performance.
prerequisites: Train/validation separation, rank statistics, multiple testing.
readFor: Trace how candidate strategies are compared across partitions and how in-sample selection is related to out-of-sample ranking. Distinguish the diagnostic from a universal probability of live failure.
limits: Author preprint is openly accessible; journal publication is 2017 and preprint dates differ. Partitioning and dependence assumptions must be assessed for your data. It does not repair look-ahead leakage or bad fills.
exercise: Generate null return series for many candidates. Compare the selected winner with an unselected candidate on a fresh period and report the full candidate count.

title: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting and Non-Normality
authors: David H. Bailey and Marcos López de Prado
why: A primary treatment of why a selected Sharpe ratio needs adjustment for search and distributional characteristics.
prerequisites: Sharpe ratio, sampling variation, skewness, kurtosis and selection bias.
readFor: Identify the benchmark against which a selected Sharpe is evaluated and the inputs reflecting the search process. Separate observed performance from confidence in an underlying effect.
limits: Author PDF verified. Trial dependence and incomplete search records complicate inputs. A favorable statistic does not establish execution feasibility, causal correctness or future stability.
exercise: Hold observed Sharpe constant while changing sample length and the number of attempted candidates. Explain why the evidence assessment should change.

title: … and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns
authors: Campbell R. Harvey, Yan Liu and Heqing Zhu
why: Explains why conventional isolated-test thresholds can be misleading when a field searches hundreds of candidate return factors.
prerequisites: Hypothesis testing, t-statistics, familywise error and false discovery.
readFor: Study the link between the number of proposed factors and the evidential hurdle. Note the role of correlated tests and the definition of the research family.
limits: 2014 working paper; published in 2016. Its proposed thresholds are model-dependent, not a universal rule that a t-statistic above three proves an edge. Different papers debate false-discovery estimates.
exercise: Document every variation in a small research sweep. Compare unadjusted significance with a clearly stated multiple-testing correction and discuss dependence.

title: Time Series Momentum
authors: Tobias J. Moskowitz, Yao Hua Ooi and Lasse H. Pedersen
why: An empirical primary paper distinguishing an instrument’s own return history from ranking assets against each other.
prerequisites: Excess returns, futures, volatility scaling and time-series evaluation.
readFor: Extract the universe, lookback, holding period, scaling and evaluation choices before attempting a reproduction. State precisely how time-series and cross-sectional momentum differ.
limits: Authors’ research page verified. Its historical multi-asset evidence is not evidence for an Indian intraday single-stock strategy. Costs, data access and contract rolling require separate implementation.
exercise: Write a one-page replication specification. Mark each unavailable dataset or assumption before writing code, and compare against a zero-signal baseline.

title: Momentum Crashes
authors: Kent Daniel and Tobias J. Moskowitz
why: A companion failure-mode reading: average strategy returns can hide concentrated losses in particular market environments.
prerequisites: Momentum construction, drawdown, conditional risk and regression.
readFor: Inspect the definition of momentum, the periods of extreme loss and the proposed connection between market conditions and strategy exposure.
limits: NBER search metadata verified; direct page fetching returned 403 during this audit. 2014 working-paper version. Historical crash descriptions do not make future regime labels observable in advance.
exercise: Compare a strategy’s unconditional mean with outcomes in a predeclared stress subset. Then build a causal state estimate and explain why it differs from hindsight classification.

title: Expected Shortfall and Beyond
why: A primary mathematical discussion of tail-risk measures and how portfolio risk can be attributed to components.
prerequisites: Quantiles, distributions, expectation and portfolio dependence.
readFor: Understand why a quantile alone leaves tail severity undescribed. Study coherence and the interpretation of risk contributions, keeping sign conventions explicit.
limits: Open author preprint verified. Mathematical properties depend on precise definitions; estimating rare tails from short market samples remains difficult. A coherent risk measure is not an accurate forecast by itself.
exercise: Construct two loss distributions with the same chosen VaR but different tail losses. Calculate their expected shortfall and explain the practical distinction.
